title: The Role of Green Artificial Intelligence in Driving Corporate Environmental Sustainability Within Society 5.0: A Theoretical Framework
abstract: Abstract This study explores the role of green artificial intelligence (green AI) in promoting environmental and institutional sustainability within the framework of Society 5.0 – a socio-technological paradigm that integrates innovation with environmental and social objectives to achieve sustainable human well-being. Green AI serves as a key enabler by reducing the ecological footprint of conventional AI systems, particularly high-energy consumption in data centres, through the adoption of energy-efficient and eco-friendly technologies. Grounded in Legitimacy Theory, Stakeholder Theory and the Resource-Based View, the study examines how Green AI adoption enhances organizational legitimacy and socio-environmental integrity. Findings indicate that institutions implementing Green AI improve their environmental and financial performance, thereby reinforcing their adaptability and credibility in increasingly sustainability-conscious regulatory environments. Theoretically, the study highlights Society 5.0’s potential to foster innovation aligned with sustainable development goals, not only by lowering carbon emissions but also by optimizing institutional processes and strengthening economic and social performance through the integration of environmental sustainability into corporate strategies. Future recommendations include conducting empirical studies to assess the impact of Green AI on environmental and financial outcomes, developing models to evaluate AI’s environmental footprint, and designing supportive public policies and regulatory incentives. Additionally, the study emphasizes the importance of examining the role of organizational culture and strengthening legislation to establish clear sustainability standards for AI development and deployment.
reason: This paper uses legitimacy as a background theoretical framework and variable in a model examining how Green AI adoption enhances organizational legitimacy, without engaging in definitional work, proposing dimensions, setting boundaries, discussing levels of analysis, or critiquing the concept of legitimacy itself. It treats legitimacy as an outcome variable rather than revising or reconceptualizing the construct.

title: Green legitimacy or greenwashing in investor relations of Indonesia’s coal mining industry
abstract: Environmental disclosure in investor relations has emerged as a critical site of legitimacy contestation in carbon-intensive industries, yet remains understudied relative to CSR and marketing communication. This study examines whether the environmental narratives of Indonesia’s five largest coal companies — ADRO, BUMI, ITMG, PTBA, and INDY — constitute substantive green legitimacy or symbolic greenwashing in investor-facing communications between 2019 and 2023. Drawing on legitimacy theory and the substantive-symbolic distinction, a Green Legitimacy-Greenwashing (GL-GW) Index is constructed using ten indicators derived from international disclosure standards (GRI, TCFD, ISSB) and Indonesia’s institutional context (PROPER, ISO 14001), applying thematic content analysis, a quantitative scorecard, and a claim-evidence matrix with intercoder reliability of Krippendorff’s Alpha >0.80. Three findings emerge: GL-GW scores ranging from 62 to 82 within a single regulatory jurisdiction confirm that regulatory homogeneity does not produce disclosure convergence; state ownership correlates consistently with more substantive disclosure, suggesting ownership-linked accountability structures moderate disclosure quality; and post-2021 score improvements concentrated in internationally exposed firms coincide with COP26 and ISSB establishment, indicating that global capital market signals are more proximate drivers of disclosure improvement than domestic regulatory compliance. The GL-GW Index offers a replicable framework transferable to other extractive sectors and emerging market contexts.
reason: This paper uses legitimacy as a variable to measure substantive vs. symbolic legitimacy in corporate disclosures, applying existing legitimacy theory to a new empirical context. While it develops a measurement index (GL-GW Index), it does not revise or argue about what legitimacy itself is as a construct. The paper treats legitimacy and greenwashing as background theoretical concepts to operationalize rather than engaging in definitional, dimensional, or boundary work on the construct of legitimacy itself. This falls under the exclusion criterion of 'measures legitimacy with an existing instrument in a new sample' and 'uses legitimacy as a variable in a model without engaging its meaning.'

title: Challenging intermediation in innovation ecosystems: towards a new multidimensional taxonomy
abstract: Innovation ecosystems are becoming increasingly critical for addressing complex societal challenges, yet they often fail due to their governance rigidity. While the literature acknowledges the importance of intermediaries, it often treats intermediation as a static role performed by fixed entities, failing to account for how coordination needs evolve as ecosystems mature. This paper challenges the static view by suggesting an adaptive intermediation perspective. Building on ecosystem governance and legitimacy dynamics, we argue that creating legitimacy conditions is what intermediaries can do. Legitimacy is derived from demonstrable coordination value, such as friction reduction, resource mobilization, and bottleneck resolution. It enables intermediaries to sustain brokerage in stable conditions and to shift toward more directive integration as urgency increases. The paper develops a conceptual framework to a set of propositions that clarify conditions under which different intermediation configurations become feasible and how governance mechanisms should be aligned accordingly. By foregrounding legitimacy as a missing aspect in processual accounts of intermediation, the study offers a complementary explanation for emerging intermediary role configurations by suggesting a new multidimensional taxonomy of intermediation to explain governance mechanisms in innovation ecosystems.
reason: Uses legitimacy as an enabling condition/variable in ecosystem intermediation governance; does not define, redefine, dimensionalize, or critique the legitimacy construct itself.

title: Crisis governance, legitimacy, and consumer ethics in service systems
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how crisis-related service restrictions shape ethical consumer responses, challenging the assumption that restrictive governance inherently promotes responsibility. It develops a dual-process model explaining how legitimacy and autonomy perceptions condition ethical engagement and resistance in service systems under crisis. Design/methodology/approach Building on a combined semi-systematic and integrative literature review, the study uses a mixed-method design integrating online discourse analysis and survey data from international consumers, using tourism as an illustrative service context. Findings Restrictive service measures fragment ethical legitimacy rather than uniformly enhancing responsibility, producing stances ranging from legitimacy-based compliance to autonomy-driven resistance. Ethical responses are shaped more by identity-coded moral orientations and legitimacy perceptions than by demographics. Research limitations/implications The paper advances services marketing and service governance research by conceptualizing crisis governance as a customer-facing relational process. Future research should extend the model to other service sectors and organizational contexts. Practical implications Crisis governance is more effective when supported by marketing-oriented service communication that enhances legitimacy and autonomy rather than relying on enforcement alone. Social implications Overly coercive crisis governance risks undermining intrinsic responsibility and weakening collective ethical commitment in service systems. Originality/value The paper provides an empirically grounded model linking legitimacy, autonomy and ethical stance formation in crisis-governed service systems, bridging consumer ethics and services marketing.
reason: This paper uses legitimacy as a variable (examining how legitimacy perceptions condition ethical engagement and resistance) without engaging in definitional, dimensional, or boundary work on the construct itself. It applies legitimacy in a crisis governance context but does not define, redefine, propose types/dimensions, set boundaries against neighboring constructs, debate level of analysis, or review/critique the concept. This falls under the exclusion criterion of using legitimacy as a variable in a model without revising what legitimacy is.

title: Information security policy as a governance capability in politically complex legislative organizations: a tridimensional configurational model
venue: Transforming Government People Process and Policy
abstract: Purpose This conceptual paper aims to examine information security policy (ISP) in Brazilian state legislative assemblies as a formal document that may operate as an institutional governance device and, under specific conditions, become a governance capability. Design/methodology/approach The paper integrates sociological institutionalism, network governance and state-capacity perspectives, in dialogue with governance-oriented information security scholarship, to theorize the conditions under which ISP may become institutionalized. Findings It develops the tridimensional model of legislative information governance (MTGIL), structured around institutional legitimacy, cross-functional coordination and political-administrative capacity and proposes three ideal-type configurations: symbolic compliance, institutional transition and substantive governance. Five testable propositions are derived. Research limitations/implications MTGIL is conceptual and untested. Its propositions, profile classifications and portability beyond Brazilian state legislative assemblies require comparative validation. Practical implications MTGIL offers legislative organizations a diagnostic lens for comparing formal ISP adoption with observable evidence of sponsorship, cross-functional routines, reporting channels, training uptake and continuity mechanisms, thereby informing policy redesign, coordination and continuity planning. Social implications By treating ISP as a governance capability, the paper suggests how legislative organizations may diagnose vulnerabilities affecting citizens’ data rights, democratic accountability and the transparency-confidentiality balance. Originality/value The paper distinguishes ISP as a formal document, an institutional governance device and a potential governance capability. MTGIL theorizes why similar policy documents, control frameworks or compliance scores may follow different institutionalization trajectories when legitimacy, coordination and capacity are configured differently.
reason: While the paper engages with institutional legitimacy as one dimension of a governance model, it does not do conceptual work on the construct of legitimacy itself. The paper uses legitimacy as a variable/component in its tridimensional model (alongside coordination and capacity) without defining, redefining, dimensionalizing, bounding, or critiquing the concept of legitimacy. It treats legitimacy as a background institutional concept rather than revising what legitimacy is or how it should be understood.

title: Legitimacy Under Algorithmic Authority: A Relational Diagnostic of Leadership Education in AI‐Mediated Contexts
abstract: As algorithmic systems become embedded in leadership development, evaluation, and recognition, they increasingly shape how authority is formed and justified. This manuscript argues algorithmic authority poses a legitimacy challenge for leadership education, especially when judgment is co-produced by humans and systems. It introduces the Surface-Cultural-Institutional-Systemic (SCIS) framework as a diagnostic lens for examining how legitimacy is configured, misaligned, or strained within hybrid authority systems. Rather than prescribing AI use or attributing legitimacy to algorithmic systems, I position leadership education as a formative but bounded site for cultivating conceptual readiness to interpret legitimacy as relational, contested, and mediated.
reason: Leadership education context; proposes a diagnostic framework for algorithmic authority legitimacy, not a redefinition of organizational legitimacy construct (borderline non-organizational legitimacy without bearing on organizational legitimacy concept).

title: Harmonizing Dual Identities via Storytelling: An Examination of Social Enterprise Storytelling in Thailand
abstract: Storytelling serves as a vital strategic communication tool for social impact organizations, particularly social enterprises that integrate both social and commercial missions within their business models. Despite the importance of storytelling in conveying hybrid identities, research on social enterprise storytelling – particularly in relation to digital communication applications – remains scarce. This study first examines the extent to which business and social narratives are employed in social enterprise storytelling and their relationship with social enterprise legitimacy. Second, it investigates storytelling approaches and the use of digital media for communication. Finally, it assesses how social enterprise legitimacy influences consumers’ perceptions of quality and value, as well as their willingness to purchase social enterprise products. Using a mixed-methods approach involving five social entrepreneurs and 211 consumers, the findings reveal that Thai social enterprises adopt a balanced use of business and social narratives, emphasizing emotional engagement over traditional storytelling elements. Both cognitive and moral legitimacy significantly influence perceived quality, with moral legitimacy exerting a stronger effect. Perceived quality mediates the relationship between legitimacy and willingness to pay. Digital innovations, including the metaverse, emerge as important communication channels. Theoretically, the study positions legitimacy as the strategic communication mechanism linking storytelling to consumer behavior. It is also among the first to combine established legitimacy and storytelling theories into a single framework and to test that framework empirically from both sides of the communication – the social entrepreneurs who craft the narratives and the consumers who receive them. Overall, the results suggest that balanced narratives and emotional engagement effectively communicate hybrid identities while enhancing consumer support.
reason: This paper uses legitimacy as a variable (antecedent to perceived quality and willingness to pay) in a model of social enterprise storytelling effectiveness, without engaging in conceptual work that defines, redefines, dimensions, bounds, or reviews the construct of legitimacy itself. It measures legitimacy with existing instruments (cognitive and moral legitimacy dimensions) in a new sample. The paper does not revise understanding of what legitimacy is.

title: Identity work as institutional navigation under racialized governance: Black African immigrant entrepreneurs in the United Kingdom
abstract: Black African immigrant entrepreneurs in the United Kingdom operate in racialized and fragmented institutional environments that systematically undermine their credibility. Focusing on the West Midlands, this article examines how identity work enables institutional navigation within these racialized governance conditions over time. Drawing on a two-phase narrative interview study with 32 entrepreneurs, the analysis draws on mixed embeddedness, critical race theory, postcolonial perspectives and identity work to explain how individuals construct self-positioning, engage regulatory, financial and community actors, and mobilize transnational ties to secure recognition and legitimacy. The article contributes to immigrant and ethnic minority entrepreneurship by conceptualizing identity work as a strategic mechanism of institutional navigation under racialized governance, by introducing a temporal and processual micro-foundation for mixed embeddedness, and by showing how transnational networks support hybrid legitimacy across fragmented regulatory contexts. The study advances understanding of entrepreneurship in unequal institutional settings while applying intersectionality as a secondary analytic lens.
reason: Studies legitimation/identity work tactics in a specific setting; uses legitimacy as an outcome without defining or revising the construct.

title: Informal Authority, Legitimacy Transition, and Institutional Change: A Theory of Advisory Capture
abstract: ABSTRACT How do informal actors achieve rapid bureaucratic dismantlement without formal authority? Analyzing the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) initiative, this article argues that when performance‐based legitimacy displaces procedural legitimacy as the dominant evaluative framework, informal actors can bypass established safeguards and reshape government institutions. Three concepts capture this process: advisory capture , legitimacy regime transition , and constrained coercion . The analysis reveals that dismantlement targets agencies based on political vulnerability rather than functional logic, that informal authority becomes institutionalized through formal rulemaking such as the Schedule Policy/Career rule, and that judicial review operates as ongoing contestation rather than definitive constraint. Protecting democratic governance requires defending not only formal rules but the legitimacy regimes within which those rules derive meaning.
reason: Introduces 'legitimacy regime transition' and contrasts performance- vs procedural-based legitimacy, which could count as proposing types/dynamics of the construct, but it is primarily a case analysis of bureaucratic dismantlement (legitimation in a political setting) and it is unclear whether it revises the concept in ways bearing on organizational legitimacy (borderline rule).

title: Oscillatory entrepreneurial identity formation: legitimacy work in university commercialisation programmes
venue: International Journal of Entrepreneurial Behaviour & Research
abstract: Purpose This micro-level study investigates how early career researchers (ECRs) in science disciplines navigate the institutional push toward commercialisation and entrepreneurial identity adoption. While entrepreneurial university institutional discourse encourages a seamless transition from scientist to entrepreneur, ECRs may experience this process as an ongoing negotiation marked by identity ambiguity and oscillation. The study addresses a gap in the literature by theorising the temporal and relational complexity of entrepreneurial identity formation in academic settings by key actors within entrepreneurial universities. Design/methodology/approach The research employs a longitudinal narrative inquiry focused on ECRs participating in a UK university's commercialisation programme. Through in-depth interviews and participant observation, the study captures how participants construct, contest, and reconfigure their identities over time in response to intersecting legitimacy demands. Findings The study introduces the concept of Oscillatory Entrepreneurial Identity Formation, theorising identity work as a multi-phase, recursive process. Rather than progressing linearly toward a stable entrepreneurial identity, participants move through three recursive overlapping phases: (1) legitimacy disruption and identity tension, (2) threshold activation and agency assertion, and (3) long-term reconciliation of plural identity futures. Identity formation is enacted provisionally, relationally and contextually, shaped by socio-institutional, collective, and internal legitimacy dynamics. Originality/value This study advances a processual model of entrepreneurial identity that challenges linear transition frameworks by recognising oscillation as a legitimate developmental trajectory. It introduces the concept of legitimacy architectures, showing how institutional, relational, and disciplinary factors shape the credibility of entrepreneurial identity claims. The findings suggest that universities can better support ECRs by reshaping socialisation processes and recognising commercial activities, enabling researchers to pursue societal impact and value creation without relinquishing their disciplinary identities.
reason: This paper uses legitimacy as a variable and background assumption to explain entrepreneurial identity formation processes in academic settings. While it discusses 'legitimacy work' and 'legitimacy architectures,' it does not engage in definitional or conceptual work on legitimacy itself—it does not define, redefine, dimensionalize, bound, or review the construct of legitimacy. Instead, it applies legitimacy concepts to understand how ECRs navigate identity adoption, treating legitimacy as a mechanism driving identity dynamics rather than examining what legitimacy is as a construct.

title: Perceived language legitimacy as a psychological judgment: a conceptual analysis of recognition, belonging, and self-worth
abstract: This article develops perceived language legitimacy (PLL) as a theoretically refined framework for examining how languages and varieties come to be regarded as authoritative, valuable, or marginal within particular social contexts. Existing accounts of language attitudes, symbolic power, and language ideology have provided important explanations of linguistic evaluation and inequality. Less attention, however, has been given to the psychological appraisal through which speakers anticipate whether a language or variety will be accepted as a credible resource for knowledge, identity, authority, or public participation within a particular domain. PLL is conceptualized as a context-sensitive psychological judgment that complements these existing sociolinguistic and social-psychological accounts by explaining how historically established hierarchies, normative expectations, identity positions, and unequal distributions of symbolic value are interpreted by speakers. It provides a psychological link between socially organized linguistic hierarchies and speakers' expectations of recognition or devaluation as language users. The article situates PLL in relation to established concepts including language attitudes, prestige, ideology, and identity. It further considers how legitimacy judgements may influence belonging, self-worth, educational uptake, public voice, and participation in multilingual societies. By focusing on this psychological interface, the article provides an account of how linguistic inequalities are experienced by speakers and translated into language-related expectations and actions.
reason: This paper develops a framework for perceived language legitimacy in sociolinguistic contexts (language varieties, multilingual societies, speakers' psychological judgments about languages). While it does definitional and conceptual work on legitimacy, it applies the construct to languages rather than organizations. Per the borderline criteria, papers on legitimacy of things other than organizations are included only if they revise the concept in a way that bears on organizational legitimacy. This paper's focus on psychological judgment of language acceptance and speaker identity in linguistic contexts does not engage with or revise organizational legitimacy theory or its application to organizational contexts.

title: Leadership under value pluralism: managing sustainability trade-offs
abstract: Purpose This paper reconceptualizes sustainability leadership as a process of decision-making under value pluralism, where leaders must navigate persistent trade-offs among legitimate but incommensurable economic, social and environmental values. It aims to advance sustainability leadership theory by demonstrating how leaders recognize, interpret and respond to conflicting demands. Design/methodology/approach A conceptual framework is created that identifies three trade-off domains, i.e. internal, external and temporal, and proposes four typical decision-making strategies, i.e. integrative, compromise, sacrificial and symbolic. To demonstrate and improve the theory, a vignette-based experiment with 412 managers manipulated regulatory enforcement, stakeholder pressure and organizational slack to see how these factors influence strategic decision-making. Findings The results demonstrate that strong enforcement increased sacrificial decisions, organizational slack enabled integrative solutions and stakeholder pressure reduced symbolic responses. Integrative and sacrificial strategies were consistently judged as more legitimate and beneficial for long-term reputation and performance than compromise or symbolic approaches. These findings provide behavioral evidence that leadership decisions in sustainability are contingent upon institutional, organizational and individual contexts. Originality/value By embedding leadership within the dynamics of decision-making under value conflict, this paper shifts the focus from harmonization to trade-offs. It specifies multilevel mechanisms and boundary conditions that shape the effectiveness of different decision strategies, offering a more realistic, context-sensitive and pluralistic account of sustainability leadership. This contribution enriches decision-making theory in management by explaining how leaders handle complex, ambiguous and morally significant choices in sustainability contexts.
reason: This paper uses legitimacy as an outcome variable in a model testing how decision-making strategies are 'judged as more legitimate' depending on contextual factors. It does not define, redefine, dimensionalize, bound, or critique the construct of legitimacy itself. The paper treats legitimacy as a dependent variable to be measured and explained rather than engaging in conceptual work on what legitimacy is or how it should be understood.

title: Islamic Business Ethics, Muslim Feminism, and the Rhetorical Construction of Entrepreneurial Legitimacy: Evidence from Emirati Women
abstract: Abstract Despite the United Arab Emirates’ state-led promotion of women’s entrepreneurship as central to national transformation, Emirati women entrepreneurs continue to face patriarchal norms that frame entrepreneurship as a masculine domain, rendering their entrepreneurial legitimacy both precarious and contested. Based on in-depth interviews, this study examines how women entrepreneurs construct entrepreneurial legitimacy within a patriarchal Muslim context, marked by a tension between empowerment rhetoric and gendered constraints. Drawing on Suddaby and Greenwood’s (2005) framework of rhetorical legitimation together with Islamic business ethics and Muslim feminism, we demonstrate how Emirati women entrepreneurs mobilise state-led empowerment and national transformation discourses to construct entrepreneurial legitimacy. We show how they align their entrepreneurship with national development goals through teleological strategies and with globalisation through cosmological strategies. We also reveal how they employ historical strategies that draw on both Emirati and Islamic history to legitimate their entrepreneurial pursuits. The analysis further reveals how Emirati, Muslim women entrepreneurs employ a Muslim feminist perspective, reinterpreting Islamic principles and business ethics to affirm their agency and inform their ontological and value-based strategies, thereby positioning their entrepreneurship as morally grounded and socially responsible. At the intersection of Islamic business ethics, Muslim feminism, and rhetorical legitimation, our analysis reveals how rhetorical legitimacy in patriarchal religious contexts depends on prior, often invisible, feminist ethical interpretation of religious texts, thereby positioning interpretative agency as a precondition for rhetorical legitimation. This study advances scholarship on women’s entrepreneurship, business ethics, and religion by demonstrating how legitimacy is constructed through interpretative work that reconciles ethical principles with rhetorical legitimation.
reason: This paper uses legitimacy as a variable in a model (examining how women entrepreneurs construct entrepreneurial legitimacy through rhetorical strategies in a specific setting) without engaging in conceptual work on the construct itself. It applies Suddaby and Greenwood's existing framework of rhetorical legitimation to a new empirical context rather than defining, redefining, dimensionalizing, or revising the concept of legitimacy. This falls under the exclusion criterion: 'uses legitimacy as a variable... in a model without engaging its meaning' and 'studies legitimation tactics or strategies in a setting without revising what legitimacy is.'

title: The Influence of Brand–Game Congruity in the Promotional Phase of Advergames: The Role of Perceived Legitimacy
abstract: Advergames—video games created by brands to convey their message—are continuously used in advertising. As voluntary entertainment experiences, their success depends on both in-game engagement and pre-play promotion. This research examines how brand–game congruity influences consumer responses in the promotional phase. Three experimental studies explore the role of three types of brand–game congruity: advertising, image, and lifestyle congruity. The combined findings establish that high congruity strengthens perceived legitimacy, leading to more favorable attitudes and behavioral responses to both the brand and the game, prior to the game experience. These insights offer relevant managerial implications for optimizing both advergame promotions and advertising effectiveness.
reason: This paper uses perceived legitimacy as a dependent variable in a causal model examining the effects of brand-game congruity on consumer responses. It does not engage in conceptual work on the construct of legitimacy itself—it does not define, redefine, dimensionalize, bound, relevel, or review legitimacy. Rather, it treats legitimacy as an outcome to be measured with existing instruments in a specific context (advergame promotion), which falls under the exclusion criterion of using legitimacy as a variable in a model without engaging its meaning.

title: Legitimacy judgments of algorithmic management and gig workers' proactive service behavior: the roles of work motivation and colleague community support
abstract: Purpose As algorithmic management grows central to platform-mediated work, understanding how gig workers evaluate and respond to such systems represents an important theoretical and practical imperative. Integrating legitimacy judgment perspective and Self-Determination Theory, this study aims to investigate how workers' assessments of autonomy, privacy, and fairness legitimacy shape proactive service behavior via autonomous and controlled motivation. We further examine the moderating role of colleague community support in these linkages. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 272 food delivery riders and ride-hailing drivers in China using a three-wave time-lagged survey design. Hierarchical regression analyses and bootstrapping techniques were used to test the hypothesized direct, mediating, and moderated mediation effects. Findings Autonomy legitimacy and fairness legitimacy were positively related to proactive service behavior, whereas privacy legitimacy was negatively related. Autonomous and controlled motivation served as distinct mediating mechanisms. Furthermore, colleague community support weakened the indirect effects of legitimacy judgments through autonomous motivation but showed no significant moderating effect on the controlled motivation pathway. Originality/value This study contributes to the algorithmic management literature by showing that workers' responses depend not only on the characteristics of algorithmic systems but also on how those systems are interpreted and evaluated by workers themselves. It provides a process-based account of proactive service behavior in gig work and clarifies how informal peer support shapes worker reactions to algorithmic control.
reason: This paper uses legitimacy as a variable (antecedent predicting proactive service behavior through mediating mechanisms) without engaging in conceptual work on the construct itself. It measures legitimacy dimensions (autonomy, privacy, fairness) as independent variables in a model but does not define, redefine, propose dimensions, set boundaries, change levels of analysis, or critique the concept of legitimacy. This falls under the exclusion criterion of using legitimacy as a variable without revising what legitimacy is.

title: International strategies for new product launches in the life sciences industry: legitimation in developed and emerging markets
abstract: Purpose This study examines the challenges that multinational enterprises (MNEs) in the life sciences industry face during international product launches. It aims to understand the specific challenges MNEs confront in different national contexts and how market environments influence the product launch process and the strategies used to gain acceptance in various markets. Design/methodology/approach A case-study approach is used, with 20 interviews with key employees from multiple sites and countries within one MNE involved in launching new products. The interviews were recorded, transcribed and supplemented by internal documents. Findings The study develops a framework that summarizes key factors influencing the launch process, including pricing sensitivity, product capabilities, brand awareness and regulatory environment. It also advances a typology that categorizes markets into four distinct quadrants based on price sensitivity and brand awareness, while incorporating the regulatory environment as a key contextual characteristic shaping legitimation strategies. Originality/value This research contributes to the literature by integrating legitimation and institutional theories with marketing theory to address new product launch. It offers a framework for understanding the factors at play and proposes a typology that focuses on the complexities of launching products across different market contexts, in the heavily regulated life sciences sector.
reason: The paper studies legitimation tactics and strategies (how MNEs gain acceptance for new products in different markets) in a specific setting without revising what legitimacy itself is. It uses legitimacy as a variable or contextual factor in explaining product launch strategies, rather than engaging in conceptual work that defines, redefines, dimensionalizes, or critiques the construct of legitimacy itself.

title: Impostor-related experiences and generative AI in a Jordanian EFL writing course
abstract: This longitudinal qualitative multiple-case study examined how 24 undergraduate EFL students at a Jordanian public university experienced generative AI during a 12-week academic writing course. The multi-source dataset included successive drafts, archived ChatGPT interactions, decision logs, reflective journals, interviews, and stimulated-recall sessions. Reflexive thematic analysis was combined with episode-level tracing. Impostor phenomenon was used as a sensitizing lens rather than as a measured participant attribute. The findings showed that AI reduced immediate drafting and language difficulties but sometimes shifted uncertainty toward ownership, legitimacy, deservingness, and fear of exposure. Students did not treat AI as a consistently reliable authority; instead, they accepted, adapted, resisted, and, most frequently, verified its suggestions. Concerns about hidden expectations and imagined judgment were evident before a Kafka-focused mini-unit. After the unit, some students used terms such as hidden rules and invisible judges to express these concerns more clearly. The findings therefore suggest that Kafka provided a shared language for reflection rather than creating these concerns or causing changes in authorship. Overall, structured AI use supported more accountable textual decision-making while also generating new affective and authorship-related pressures.
reason: This paper studies generative AI in an educational writing context and examines student experiences with impostor phenomenon. It does not engage with the construct of legitimacy itself—legitimacy is mentioned only as one affective concern among others that students experienced ('uncertainty toward ownership, legitimacy, deservingness, and fear of exposure'), but the paper does not define, redefine, dimensionalize, bound, or review legitimacy as a concept. The paper uses legitimacy as a background attribute of student experience rather than doing conceptual work on the construct itself.

title: Decision substitution and the reorganisation of judgement in AI-mediated society
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly embedded in institutional and everyday contexts, where they are publicly framed as decision-support tools yet often function as de facto decision-makers. This study argues that the shift from algorithmic support to decision substitution constitutes a significant societal problem insufficiently addressed by prevailing AI ethics and governance frameworks. Rather than focussing solely on technical performance, bias, or transparency, the analysis examines how AI-mediated practices reconfigure human agency, responsibility, and judgement. Drawing on philosophy of technology and socio-technical scholarship, it conceptualises AI systems as cultural and epistemic infrastructures that shape how knowledge is produced, authority distributed, and action legitimised. It argues that AI increasingly reorganises the decision field by restructuring visibility, validation, participation, and legitimacy, thereby transforming the conditions under which judgement is exercised. The research distinguishes between decision support, decision delegation, and decision substitution, showing how human judgement can be displaced even when human actors remain formally involved. The analysis identifies threshold conditions through which decision substitution emerges, including constrained dissent, diminished corrective capacity, default algorithmic legitimacy, and the separation of authority from accountability. These dynamics generate responsibility asymmetries in which accountability remains attached to human actors while authority migrates towards algorithmic systems. The problem is most acute in contexts characterised by indeterminacy, where values, tacit knowledge, and ethical concerns resist formalisation. The research concludes by advancing a society-shaping-the-algorithm perspective that reframes human-in-the-loop governance as a collective and institutional condition rather than a procedural safeguard, providing a conceptual foundation for preserving meaningful human judgement in AI-mediated societies.
reason: This paper uses legitimacy as a variable/process within a broader analysis of AI-mediated decision-making (specifically 'default algorithmic legitimacy' as a threshold condition), but does not engage in conceptual work on the construct of legitimacy itself. It does not define, redefine, dimensionalize, bound, or review legitimacy as a concept. The paper treats legitimacy as a background assumption about how AI systems gain acceptance rather than revising what legitimacy means or how we should understand it.

title: “Distributive fiscal justice” as a new dimension of corporate legitimacy in climate governance: a conceptual insight and foresight
venue: International Journal of Ethics and Systems
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this conceptual paper is to understand how corporate tax transparency shapes social equity in climate governance. Design/methodology/approach Through a qualitative, theory-building design, grounded in a systematic literature review, this study brings together environmental justice theory, legitimacy theory, institutional theory and political economy to develop an integrative conceptual framework that challenges existing assumptions, using a critical theorist standpoint. Findings The synthesis outcomes indicate that fiscal legitimacy is constituted across three interdependent dimensions – procedural, cognitive and distributive – and that prevailing environmental, social and governance (ESG) frameworks capture only the first. The study provides a normative standard for evaluating whether corporate tax practices contribute equitably to public revenues in climate-vulnerable jurisdictions. It theorises a structural fiscal-climatic injustice cycle through which corporate tax avoidance may constrain domestic adaptation finance in Global South countries, a synthesis outcome advanced as theoretically plausible rather than as an established causal claim. Research limitations/implications This study is conceptual and does not include primary empirical data, which limits the strength of causal claims. Future research should apply quantitative methodologies to test the fiscal-climatic injustice cycle and assess whether mandatory country-by-country reporting regimes demonstrably improve adaptation finance adequacy. Case study research in high-vulnerability, low-income country contexts – particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa and Small Island Developing States – is essential to operationalise distributive fiscal justice with country-specific baselines. The effective-tax-rate gap, revenue-profit alignment ratio and adaptation finance contribution gap indicators warrant testing in specific national and sectoral settings, particularly climate-vulnerable jurisdictions. Practical implications For companies, this study recommends conducting fiscal legitimacy audits and voluntarily publishing total tax contribution reports alongside sustainability disclosures. Board-level tax governance mechanisms should be established, with fiscal coherence indicators that explicitly link tax disclosures to climate policy outcomes. For ESG rating agencies and standard setters, the study provides a blueprint for integrating a distributive fiscal justice pillar into assessment architectures. For governments in developing countries, corporate fiscal responsibility should be recognised as a climate finance issue. United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change negotiations should incorporate corporate tax transparency provisions into climate finance mechanisms. Social implications The study highlights structural harms that disproportionately affect communities in the Global South. It identifies this harm as a manifestation of distributive injustice and incorporates it into ESG governance discourse, thereby generating normative pressure for systemic reform. Repositioning corporate fiscal conduct as a social equity issue has the potential to shift the terms of climate finance advocacy, empowering affected communities and their governments to make legitimate claims about the fiscal contributions of companies operating within their borders. Originality/value The study proposes a construct dubbed “distributive fiscal justice”, a new sub-dimension of fiscal legitimacy that captures the equity implications of corporate tax behaviour and links individual company behaviour to collective climate vulnerability. It reveals areas where the prevailing ESG and corporate social responsibility disclosure frameworks fall short of equity demands. It positions tax transparency as a non-negotiable foundation for equitable climate governance. It offers five theoretical propositions that inform the empirical agenda and policy reform.
reason: Conceptual paper that proposes a new dimension/sub-dimension of corporate legitimacy ('distributive fiscal justice' within fiscal legitimacy), i.e., revises types/dimensions of the construct.

title: The ‘failed researcher’ – perceptions of illegitimacy and the marginalisation of education focused academics in Australia
abstract: Abstract For many academics, appointment to an education focused (EF) role can trigger a sense of illegitimacy and professional marginalisation. This experience is not universal, but it is reported repeatedly in the literature. Whilst existing research has documented these experiences, less attention has been paid to how they are institutionally produced and sustained. This paper addresses this gap by examining the institutional construction of EF academics’ perceived illegitimacy within Australian universities. Drawing on interview data and neo-institutional theory, the study identifies a recurring conception of the EF academic as the ‘failed researcher’. Within this institutional identity category, the EF academic’s focus on teaching and students’ learning is framed not as specialisation, but as deviation from the idealised research-active norm. It shapes EF academics’ experiences in overt and covert ways, through workload practices, promotion processes, informal interactions, and organisational cultures, contributing to patterns of exclusion across many universities. These experiences are both context-bound and -agnostic – embedded in local organisational environments, yet recurrent across the sector. Importantly, EF academics’ diverse motivations and expertise challenge the validity of the ‘failed researcher’ conception. Rather than reflecting the realities of EF academic work, it functions as an influential institutional logic through which legitimacy is evaluated. By examining how perceptions of legitimacy may be institutionally constructed, this paper advances understanding of why formally differentiated academic roles may nevertheless remain hierarchically valued. The paper concludes that positioning EF academics as ‘failed researchers’ is not only unjust and unsupported by evidence, but also increasingly untenable within contemporary universities.

title: Managing sustainability under uncertainty: how executive paradoxical cognition shapes dynamic capabilities and ESG outcomes
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how sustainability initiatives are shaped under conditions of regulatory ambiguity and market turbulence, focusing on how executive paradoxical cognition influences the activation of dynamic capabilities and the translation of internal adaptation into externally recognized environmental, social and governance (ESG) legitimacy. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a sequential mixed-methods design combining a sector-wide survey of banking institutions with in-depth qualitative interviews across diverse ownership forms. Structural relationships are examined using partial least squares structural equation modelling, while qualitative pattern matching is used to interpret the cognitive and organizational processes underlying the observed relationships. Findings The results of this study show that environmental uncertainty strengthens paradoxical cognition, which in turn supports the activation of dynamic capabilities related to sensing, seizing and reconfiguring. Capability development alone, however, does not translate directly into enhanced ESG legitimacy. When paradoxical cognition is more pronounced, internal adaptation becomes harder to stabilize as external legitimacy, as ongoing experimentation and reconfiguration increase interpretive complexity and stakeholder scrutiny. Qualitative evidence further indicates that while paradoxical thinking facilitates learning and innovation, it can complicate the articulation of coherent and externally legible ESG narratives. Originality/value This study advances Paradox Theory by foregrounding cognitive tension as a mechanism shaping sustainability-related legitimacy processes. It also extends Dynamic Capabilities Theory by showing how capability activation unfolds under institutional constraints rather than under conditions of regulatory coherence. In doing so, this study explains why executive adaptability may simultaneously enable organizational learning and constrain legitimacy formation under uncertainty.

title: Legitimacy and conflict: academic perspectives on hybrid governance and third-space professionals in a Chilean university
venue: Perspectives Policy and Practice in Higher Education
abstract: Universities worldwide are experiencing a rise in the professionalisation of management, leading to hybrid roles that bridge academic and administrative areas. While these third-space professionals play a vital role in coordinating institutions, their legitimacy remains contested, and their contributions are inconsistently recognised. Based on sixteen semi-structured interviews with academics and academic officials at a Chilean university, this article explores how legitimacy and conflict are relationally constructed between academics and these professionals, from the academics’ perspective. By combining these interviews with document analysis, it introduces a four-scenario model – Effective Collaboration, Active Institutional Conflict, Invisibility, and Identity Conflict and Resistance – to analyse how legitimacy is negotiated and how conflicts arise in hybrid governance. The findings suggest that legitimacy is dynamic and relational, influenced by organisational culture, leadership, and symbolic hierarchies. Although managerial reforms improve coordination, they also heighten tensions over academic autonomy, leading to fluctuating patterns of cooperation and resistance. The four-scenario model serves as an analytical tool; in this case, the institution primarily aligns with the identity-conflict-and-resistance scenario. The study views the Chilean case as a contribution to global discussions on hybrid governance and expands Whitchurch’s framework by adding conflict intensity as a key analytical aspect. Practically, it recommends strategies such as dialogue, transparency, and shared decision-making to balance managerial skills with academic trust and support sustainable, legitimate governance in higher education.

title: ‘If We Had Known’: Whistleblowers, Animal Welfare Scandals and Agri-food Stakeholders’ Response
abstract: Abstract Farm animal welfare (FAW) scandals can impact firm legitimacy and regulatory responses in food supply chains. Yet, limited research explains how governance structures and power asymmetries influence stakeholder responses to such events. This paper provides a qualitative comparative analysis of three major FAW scandals in the dairy sector across the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada. Drawing on stakeholder and normative legitimacy theory, the study develops a conceptual framework linking whistleblower convergence, supply chain governance, and organizational response strategies. The findings show that elite downstream affiliations intensify scandal contagion, while governance structures condition whether actors pursue accommodation or decoupling strategies. Power asymmetries between upstream farms and downstream buyers further shape the distribution of legitimacy risks and corrective costs. By integrating value chain governance with legitimacy theory, the paper provides insights into how agri-food stakeholders respond to ethical crises and the implications this has for improving FAW standards across global supply chains.

title: Value creation in sport business in the age of AI: a multidimensional framework
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Sport organisations, governments, sponsors, scholars, and athletes routinely appeal to the value of sport, and they almost always mean different things. The cost of this incoherence is no longer theoretical. Artificial intelligence is now a central subject of strategic, governance, and ethical debate in sport, yet the field lacks an integrative framework to assess what AI does to the value sport creates. This paper proposes a multidimensional framework — the Sport Value Architecture — that holds value plurality, capture asymmetry, and legitimacy in a single conceptual structure, and extends it to the age of AI. Sport generates three logically distinct types of value: competitive, commercial, and social. They stand in a determinate but non-uniform order: competitive value is a strict precondition of commercial value, and it conditions, rather than founds social value, which can arise from participation alone but collapses once a claimed contest is exposed as corrupted. Each is captured asymmetrically across four stakeholder groups, anchored in an irreducible sport activity accessible through three modes (Play, Spectate, Use), conditioned by three enabling conditions (governance, environmental responsibility, equity), and located within four exogenous force fields. Legitimacy is the outcome of the model working under defensible conditions, not a fourth deliverable. AI runs through every layer simultaneously: generating value within each value type, reshaping capture across every stakeholder group, stressing every enabling condition, and pressing on the irreducible activity itself. The framework supplies the conceptual apparatus to organise the strategic, governance, and ethical decisions this moment demands.

title: Trust and sustainability in Web3 token economies: a multi-level socio-technical perspective on complex digital systems
abstract: Purpose Although token economies have become a defining feature of many Web3 platforms, their ability to sustain participation over time remains uncertain. A recurring pattern can be observed across several ecosystems: rapid initial growth is often followed by declining engagement, weakening trust, and unstable participation. This study seeks to understand why such outcomes persist despite increasingly sophisticated incentive structures. Design/methodology/approach The paper adopts a conceptual approach and develops a multi-level framework by drawing together insights from self-determination theory, agency theory, trust theory, institutional theory, platform economics and cybernetic systems thinking. Rather than viewing token economies only through market incentives, the framework examines how behavioral motivations, governance practices, institutional conditions and feedback processes interact in shaping long-term engagement. Findings The study suggests that sustained participation in token economies depends on more than financial rewards alone. Intrinsic motivations, such as community involvement and meaningful participation, appear to play an important role in maintaining engagement over time. Governance transparency and perceived fairness strengthen user trust, while trust itself emerges as a key mechanism linking platform design to continued participation. The framework further indicates that sustained engagement contributes to ecosystem stability, although these relationships are influenced by broader institutional conditions, including regulatory clarity and legitimacy. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual study, the framework has not yet been empirically tested. The propositions developed here provide a basis for future research examining how trust, motivation and governance evolve across different types of Web3 ecosystems. The paper also opens opportunities for longitudinal and comparative studies exploring the sustainability of token-based platforms under varying institutional contexts. Practical implications The findings suggest that platform designers should avoid relying exclusively on token-based incentives to drive participation. Greater attention may need to be given to governance transparency, functional token utility, community-building mechanisms, and long-term alignment among stakeholders. For policymakers, clearer and more consistent regulatory approaches may help reduce uncertainty and strengthen ecosystem credibility. Social implications The paper contributes to ongoing discussions about Web3 as a potential infrastructure for digital social innovation. By emphasizing trust, participation and institutional legitimacy, the study highlights how decentralized systems may support more collaborative and community-oriented forms of digital coordination. Originality/value This study contributes by reframing token economies as socio-technical and cybernetic systems embedded within broader institutional environments rather than treating them purely as economic mechanisms. It offers an integrated explanation of how motivation, governance, trust, legitimacy and recursive feedback interact to influence the long-term sustainability of Web3 ecosystems.

title: The moral authority of corporate codes of ethics: normative conditions for legitimate organizational norm-setting
abstract: Abstract Corporate codes of ethics (CCE) do more than express values and prescribe conduct. Through them, organizations interpret moral expectations, guide decisions, and hold agents answerable. This raises a prior philosophical question: under what conditions can an organization legitimately claim and exercise moral authority through CCE? Through a problem-driven normative reconstruction connecting business ethics with philosophical accounts of practical authority, moral justification, bounded moral pluralism, and moral agency, this article identifies five interdependent conditions: explicit moral justification; a limited and internally ordered moral core; legitimate and contestable contextual interpretation; jurisdictional and moral limits to hierarchical authority; and the orientation, support, and accountability of moral judgment. Together, these conditions form an integrated architecture linking codified moral content with organizational standing, jurisdiction, interpretive governance, and responsible agency. Their joint satisfaction supports a defeasibly legitimate claim to organizational moral authority, while particular exercises of that authority remain subject to moral assessment. By shifting normative analysis from CCE as purported bearers of authority to the organizational claim advanced and the authority exercised through them, the framework distinguishes the moral validity of prescriptions from the moral legitimacy of organizational authority and integrates moral content, organizational power, contextual interpretation, and moral agency. The article contributes to business ethics and the philosophy of management by explaining how organizational norm-setting can guide action and support accountability while remaining answerable to defensible moral reasons and responsible moral judgment.

title: Sport sponsorship and sponsorship-linked investment under Saudi Vision 2030: a PRISMA-ScR review of direct and contextual evidence on brand equity, legitimacy, and value co-creation
venue: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
abstract: Introduction Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 links sport sponsorship with commercial branding, sport-sector investment, tourism, public policy, and contested legitimacy narratives. This systematic scoping review maps direct evidence on sponsorship outcomes and distinguishes it from broader contextual scholarship. Methods Following PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidance, an updated OpenAlex search was conducted on 22 August 2026 using 11 title-and-abstract query blocks, supplemented by backward/forward citation checking and targeted searches of official sources. Of 303 records identified (289 database hits and 14 supplementary records), 89 duplicates/duplicate versions were removed, leaving 214 records for screening. Thirty-seven full texts were assessed and 27 reports were included: six direct sponsorship studies and 21 contextual studies or reports. General theory sources were used only for interpretation. Results Direct evidence, concentrated in football and dominated by cross-sectional, purposive, or qualitative designs, links sponsorship awareness and identification with sponsor image, attitude, purchase intention, and, more recently, stakeholder resistance to sponsor legitimacy. Contextual evidence maps modernization, soft-power, sportswashing, tourism, participation, and governance mechanisms but does not identify sponsorship effects. Study-level appraisal indicates moderate-to-high concern across most direct studies because of non-probability sampling, self-report measurement, narrow settings, or interpretive dependence. Discussion The synthesis supports an evidence-calibrated framework in which audience processing explains near-term brand outcomes, while governance credibility and stakeholder participation are proposed boundary conditions for legitimacy and public value. These latter pathways, and the proposed measurement dashboard, remain author-derived propositions requiring direct empirical validation.

title: Intersectionality, legitimacy and women's digital leadership in AI-enabled workplaces: a systematic review
venue: Equality Diversity and Inclusion An International Journal
abstract: Purpose This paper examines how legitimacy mediates the relationship between structural inequalities and women's digital leadership (WDL) in AI-enabled workplaces. It focuses on how academic and organizational knowledge constructs inclusion and exclusion, particularly through structural inequality, algorithmic bias, and governance related to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 5 and 10. Design/methodology/approach The study combines a systematic literature review, science mapping, and variable science mapping of 581 Scopus-indexed journal articles published from 2000 to September 2025. Article-level verification identified 27 potential integrative matches, of which three substantively addressed women or gender, leadership or managerial authority, and AI-enabled or digitally mediated workplace systems concurrently. These three studies constitute the direct WDL evidence, whereas the wider 581-article corpus maps the interdisciplinary foundations surrounding this emerging domain. Findings Evidence from the three-study direct core indicates that gender, managerial authority, and digitally mediated workplace systems rarely converge within a single empirical design. The broader interdisciplinary corpus identifies recurring structural, technological, and institutional asymmetries, together with reflexive leadership, responsible AI governance, and inclusive institutional redesign. Integrating these adjacent patterns through organizational legitimacy clarifies how resource allocation, decision processes, meaning-making, and normative validation may shape WDL across global, national, organizational, and individual levels. Originality/value The paper offers a legitimacy-centered synthesis of WDL in AI-enabled workplaces. Its contribution is conceptual rather than causal: it explains how intersectional positions, organizational power, and AI-mediated knowledge may jointly shape recognition and exclusion. This framing connects diversity, equality, and inclusion (DEI) research with organizational legitimacy and critical algorithm studies.

title: Turkey-European Union relations in world polity
venue: Royal Holloway Digital Repository (Royal Holloway University of London)
abstract: By 'bringing in' the global dimension, this thesis aims to explain the main reasons for Turkey's failure to comply with EU conditionality. Existing studies in the field either look at the hardships in Turkish-EU intergovernmental bargains or at the 'cultural mismatch' that triggers opposition in the conservative circles of both Turkey and Europe. Such tendencies mislead many students to miss the 'bigger picture'; in other words, the global legitimation processes underlying Turkey's interactions with the EU. By introducing World Polity theory, an innovative sociological institutionalist theory developed by a Stanford University sociologist, John W. Meyer, since the 19705, this thesis promises a fuller analysis of the difficult relations between Turkey and the EU through the study of three key sectors where EU-led reforms prove particularly problematic: foreign land ownership, ombudsmanship, and Turkey's Cyprus policy. Benefiting from original interview and survey findings, the thesis demonstrates that the likelihood of EU-led reform depends on the extent to which it is perceived as globally legitimate in the candidate country, Turkey. The main argument is that Turkey-European Union relations should be considered within the context of a wider global cultural environment in which they are deeply embedded and which constitute their agency. This argument is innovative in three ways. First, it adds the global context, which is severely neglected in the prevailing studies on EU-Turkey relations, as a constitutive element to the analysis. Second, it offers new analytical tools to rethink the EU as an 'organizational carrier' of world models and better explain the domestic motivations behind compliance with EU conditionality. Finally, it contributes to World Polity research that is increasingly criticized for having a top-down approach and lacking in-depth case studies on how world models spread.

title: International film festivals as field-configuring events
abstract: Studies examining the issue of organizational field evolution, especially on cultural field's, have found that some events shape the process by acting as 'purveyors of legitimacy' (Anand and Peterson, 2000). However, no research is forthcoming on events such as international film festivals that serve a similar function. A new theoretical framework - field-configuring events (FCEs) by Lampel' and Meyer (2008) seeks to rectify the lack of attention paid to 'events' by organization scientists. . Adopting their framework, my research explicates one such event in cultural industries, particularly the global film in9ustry - international filin festival. Towards that end, my PhD thesis spawns four papers - one conceptual and three empirical papers. First, I articulate international film festivals as field-configuring events, and identify some of their key characteristics: spatial embededness, temporal recurrence, programming, premiership, juried competition, film markets, side bars, and accreditation. Second, I examine the organization, strategy, and performance of international film festivals. I propose that a prototypical international film festival is a competition of 'films, and its perfonnance is dependent on two resource streams: reputation of nominated films/film makers, and reputation of members of the jury panel. Third, I explicate the macro linkages between an FCE and national film institutions such as BFI through a process known as retrospective consecration. I propose that international film festivals such as Cannes, Venice, and Berlin directly impact.BFI's efforts of anointing the best British films of the 20th century or 'BFI Top Ido'. Finally, I focus on the micro linkages between international film festivals and BFI choices, particularly focusing on how the. choices emerge from a voting college. The BFI's 'Top 100' voting college consists of three groups of respondents or 'cultural hierarchies' - experts, peers, and the public, and I propose that international film festivals represent a fonn of critical recognition and shape expert choices. title: Evaluations as Mirrors and Co-constructors : An Empirical Investigation of a Microfinance Rating Agency and its Rating Practices from 1999–2014
abstract: Microfinance has been hailed as a “magic bullet” for poverty alleviation and women’s empowerment, and many believe that microfinance organizations (MFOs) can help the world’s poor move up the socioeconomic ladder. However, MFOs are also under increasing pressure to demonstrate high levels of organizational efficiency, economies of scale, and strong financials. The expectations facing these organizations are thus inherently contradictory: MFOs must do good and at the same time do well.In this dissertation, I focus on the expectations and demands imposed on MFOs by external evaluators. More specifically, I investigate how rating practices and the idealized organizational images that these project were constructed and worked in the Indian microfinance sector from 1999-2014. Through their credit recommendations, rating agencies not only direct the flow of resources in the market; their assessments also constitute a type of normative guidance for MFOs, signaling a set of criteria and ideals for how organizations should act and be structured, as well as which goals should be prioritized and pursued.In my analysis, I identify three sequential and distinct idealized images which are encoded in the rating reports during the study period. This means that ratings lead to the reinforcement of one particular model of conducting microfinance. I also find that prominent raters play a dual role. First, they inform MFOs about the idealized image by codifying what “is out there”, thus explicating institutional pressures. At the same time, they also actively contribute to the construction of idealized images, thereby suggesting which organizations and organizational features should be bestowed with legitimacy. The construction of the idealized image is found to be more noticeable during the early years of the study period, when the field was newly emerging.

title: Legitimizing e-social capital cues' integration:investigating the multiple paths of resistance among web designers
abstract: Objectives Web site design is often portrayed as a key tool in attracting customers and in providing sustainable competitive advantage to e-firm (Dailey 2004; Eroglu, Machleit, and Davis 2001). While most of the e-marketing research has tended to concentrate on deterministic aspects of websites such as navigation, search, payment convenience and generic atmospherics like colors, designers‟ resistance and lack of explicit legitimacy for the inclusion of social cues seem to be present (deKervenoael et al, 2009). Yet, the importance of effectively dealing with socially oriented design variables and social capital has been proven to naturally increase international market share as demonstrated by several studies (Constantinides, 2004; Klein, 2003) and reflected in the success of social networking sites. In this context, our paper analyses: how web designers through their daily practices, adopt recursive, adaptive and resisting behavior regarding the inclusion of social cues online and shape the socio-technical power relationship between designers and clients. Methods We explore qualitatively three types of emerging resistance namely: market driven resistance, ideological resistance and functional resistance Vignettes through a think aloud techniques are used (Miles and Huberman, 1994; Preissle et al, 1997) and follow Yin (1994) pattern matching strategy. The findings and analysis proceed concurrently with theorizing. Findings The vignettes demonstrate that designers' social context is important in shaping web site design. The findings point out at multiples paths of resistance not to include social capital. In turn, most type of resistance are legitimized through external and technical variables rather than implicating directly the web designer. Towards this end, we develop a series of propositions providing a novel contribution to existing theory on the social impact of e-technologies. Conclusion The study allows further understanding of web designers‟ impact in shaping the current e-development tools such as Web 3.0, also named the semantic web or smart web, which includes advanced social capital features socially grounded within consumers‟ day to day environment and practices. We argue that further social skills ought to be acquired by web designers and explicitly made visible in their design. These in turn, will create sustainable differentiation strategies in the profession creating a two tier market whereby some designers are able to provide inimitable value added services within specific markets while other only provide basic technical services.

title: Early Adoption Dynamics Of Private Sustainability Governance Initiatives: A Case Study Of The Marine Cultured-Pearl Industry
venue: ScholarWorks -A service of University of Vermont Libraries (University of Vermont)
abstract: We are witnessing a time of unprecedented human impact on the natural environment. Coral reefs, one of the most biologically diverse and productive ecosystems, are at the forefront of enduring these human impacts. Despite widespread recognition of coral reef degradation, counter measures have not reached a scale to offset the threat. The magnitude of this and other environmental issues call for a deeper understanding of the role the private sector can play in sustainable development. In response to environmental pressures and the shortcomings of global-scale governance, private sustainability governance initiatives have developed. In the last decade, these initiatives have flourished, resulting in a diversity of formats including third-party certification, consumer product transparency systems, and industry roundtables. In many industries, these programs compete to define the transformation and evolution of sustainability governance in an industry. This dissertation draws on a case study of the marine cultured-pearl industry to highlight the early adoption dynamics of private sustainability governance initiatives. The marine cultured-pearl industry provides an illuminating case study for the adoption of private governance, based on the potential strength of the positive environmental impact and farm presence in ecologically vulnerable coral reef areas. Yet despite these strengths, no formal sustainability initiatives have developed. This research project explores the early adoption of private governance initiatives through a mixed-methodological, case-study approach. The first study, a quantitative survey of US jewelry consumers, examines the impacts of environmental messages on perceptions of luxury value. The second study assesses the effect of networked legitimacy on producer perceptions in private governance initiatives. The final study investigates the impact of value chain structure on competing private governance initiatives. The research results provide evidence of a strong business case for the development of industry-wide sustainability initiatives and highlights distinctions between the rival private governance initiatives. The US jewelry consumer research shows that consumer messages featuring sustainability standards to protect coral reefs outperform third-party certification on luxury attributes. The marine cultured-pearl producer research highlights the legitimacy advantages of consumer product transparency when compared to third-party certifications. The value chain research indicates that, when compared to third-party certifications, consumer product transparency systems have characteristics that provide an advantage in addressing producer upgrading opportunities. Results from each of the three studies highlight the potential advantages of consumer product transparency systems over third-party certification initiatives in this and other settings. These results helped inform participatory action research to assess alternative pathways for private sustainability governance.

title: Masked or Informed Citizens?: Social Media and Online Health Consultations
abstract: The diffusion of social media is having profound impacts on the relationship between government and citizens in many areas of government service provision. In the area of healthcare the emergence of new venues of interaction between patients and between patients and doctors is challenging the government-established digital channels for healthcare service provision. In this paper we present a classification scheme with four types of online health forums and use this framework to explore data from the Danish case that illustrates trends of cost, use, and transformation of each of the types of online health forum. Although this paper is a research in progress, we put forward the hypothesis in the paper that the uptake of social media in the health sector is being used as a way for governments and corporate forces to increase control and reinforce legitimacy, rather than empowering citizens. In the conclusion, we suggest venues of future research on this emerging trend.

title: The Process of Legitimizing Business Model Innovation - A multiple case study of Swedish and Chinese MNEs
venue: Gothenburg University Publications Electronic Archive (Gothenburg University)
abstract: Studies have shown how companies that are constantly revising and implementing business model innovations are more likely to navigate through complex environments and thus succeed in the long run. Despite this fact, the process of developing new business model innovations is faced with a wide range of illegitimacy challenges. Gaining legitimacy in the process of business model innovation (BMI) therefore becomes of vital importance. The main purpose of this qualitative multiple case study is to get a deeper understanding of illegitimacy challenges in the process of business model innovation, as well as investigating ways of gaining and/or maintaining legitimacy throughout the process. Theories indicate several illegitimacy challenges and suggestions of strategies for gaining and maintaining legitimacy. The empirical findings of this thesis confirm what previous scholars have found within the focal field. Moreover, the novel findings of this thesis contributed to the development within the field. At an initial stage of the process, it is beneficial to “work under the radar”; which gives the project time to mature without having to meet strict deadlines and challenging opinions from established forces. Additionally, findings show how an authority figure within the organization often enhances the process of gaining legitimacy. Furthermore, the creator of the BMI project must be passionate and energetic about the innovation, as well as being prepared to invest the time needed to structure clear and realistic goals for the business model innovation project. Lastly, this thesis shows the importance of protecting recent accomplishment to strengthen legitimacy gained within the organization in the long run.

title: Strategies of legitimation in sex education texts
venue: University of Birmingham Institutional Research Archive (University of Birmingham)
abstract: This study seeks to investigate strategies of legitimation within the politically sensitive subject of sex education. Sex and Relationships Education (SRE) is one of the few areas of the present UK school curriculum which is not compulsory, and which contains a parental right to withdrawal of their child. The thesis looks at how arguments are marshalled in a small set of sex education manuals for British teenagers for the purpose of legitimating the subject to a potentially ambivalent readership. Legitimation strategies are identified within the texts and then broken down into their composite parts using the recently-developed argumentation framework created by Fairclough and Fairclough (2012). It is argued that the framework can be extended for use beyond their own remit of political texts, and that this can provide analysts of educational texts with a useful tool for investigating latent discourses.
